newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil oil deregulation faces key vote in Congress.
newsitem.headline: Brazil oil deregulation faces key vote in Congress.

text.p: A bill opening up Brazil's oil and gas industry to private competition was due to be put to a full vote in the Chamber of Deputies on Wednesday, the biggest step yet towards deregulating the country's petroleum sector.

It has been nearly a year and a half since Congress approved a constitutional amendment doing away with the state's oil and gas monopoly. And lawmakers have been arguing for months over the details of the regulatory legislation.

A committee in Brazil's lower legislative house, the Chamber of Deputies, finally approved the legislation Tuesday. But differences remain over crucial questions, such as the possibility of privatizing state-owned Petrobras.

Leaders of allied parties were due to meet to seek agreement on the bill before a lower house session to vote on it began at 1600 local/1900 GMT. Newspapers said there was a possibility the vote could be delayed until next week.
The bill as it stands would allow private firms to compete or enter joint-ventures with Petrobras, sets up a new sector regulator and scraps fuel price subsidies within three years.
Petrobras is seen as the main beneficiary of the new law which would let it keep Brazil's richest oil and gas fields.

Petrobras would be freed of bureaucratic shackles that traditionally hamper state-owned companies. It would hand over to the new sector regulator its duty of making sure fuel gets to Brazil's most remote communities.
It would also be allowed to enter joint ventures with the private sector, as a majority or minority partner, and sell off assets without approval from Congress on each occasion.

With 40 years experience as the sole prospector and producer of oil and gas in Brazil, and a recognized leader in deepwater technology needed for the country's offshore reserves, Petrobras is expected to be in demand from would-be partners.

"Any company coming to Brazil will be knocking first on Petrobras' door to see what the conditions look like," said Gilbert Landsberg, director of corporate affairs at the Brazilian subsidiary of the Royal Dutch/Shell Group.

In a recent speech, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said Petrobras had received more than 100 proposals for joint ventures which, if implemented, would double Brazil's daily oil production currently about 860,000 barrels per day.

"Petrobras will no longer be the government's policy tool. From now on it will be the market that sets the tone and that is great news for Petrobras," said Ricardo Kobayashi, an analyst with investment bank Banco Pactual.
However, Brazil's enthusiasm for market forces has its limits -- a controversial article of the bill sets in stone the state's obligation to keep control of Petrobras.
In 1995, President Cardoso pledged Petrobras would not be privatized in order to overcome resistance to the constitutional amendment that ended the petroleum monopoly.

But members of the pro-privatization Liberal Front Party, the government's staunchest ally, intend to present an amendment to the bill that would leave Brazil free to sell off Petrobras, which is valued at about $20 billion.
Another controversial article in the bill would make distribution of fuel and natural gas, except to big industrial consumers, the exclusive right of licensed distributors.
Government and opposition lawmakers object to that clause, arguing it contradicts the bill's aim of making the petroleum industry more competitive and would add to the cost of fuel.
They have said they will support an amendment eliminating the article, leaving the matter to be decided by the new sector regulator, the National Petroleum Agency.

Private distributors already active in Brazil argue the bill in fact favors Petrobras by allowing it to sell directly to steelmakers, chemical and petrochemical producers and thermoelectric power plants.
Newspaper Gazeta Mercantil said Tuesday the distributors would seek to rewrite the bill to give them a bigger share of the market when the legislation reaches the Senate.
